newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan goes for early election.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan goes for early election.

text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, announced on Sunday he would seek early elections after months of pressure on his coalition from the secularist army.
"We decided that for Turkey to continue its economic success, an early election would be necessary," Erbakan told a news conference.
Pro-Western coalition partner Tansu Ciller, appearing with Erbakan, said she would lead a caretaker government from the end of June until parliament can set a date for new polls.
"The time of the election has not been determined for certain. It will be debated by our authorised councils, although we want it as soon as possible," Erbakan said.

His Islam-based Welfare Party is widely believed to have increased its share of the vote since it narrowly won general elections at the end of 1995 with 21 percent, but few reliable opinion polls have been published recently.

Political analysts say even govenrment MPs may be reluctant to pass the required election legislation for fear of losing their seats and the substantial privileges, including generous pension benefits and other perks, that go with them.
However, one left-wing party has urged early polls to settle the political crisis, sparked by military demands for an anti-Islamist crackdown.

Ciller's appointment as prime minister would also require MPs' approval. The 11-month-old coalition lost its absolute majority in the national assembly last week but it still has two more deputies than the opposition because of empty seats.
Turkish press reports say Erbakan, 70, wants a quick poll, but that U.S.-trained economist Ciller is holding out for a date next spring. Elections would normally be due by the year 2000.
The Welfare Party faces closure for allegedly threatening Turkey's secular system in a Constitutional Court case to be decided on in about six months.

The case is part of an assault on the Islamists by the secularist elite. The powerful army, which has staged three coups since 1960, last month declared its struggle against Islamists as a matter of "life or death" for NATO-member Turkey.
Secularist pressure diverted Erbakan, 70, from his aim of increasing the role of Islam in public life at home and getting on better terms with Turkey's Moslem neighbours.
On Sunday he predicted Welfare and Ciller's True Path Party would get a firmer mandate after going to the nation.
"We believe we (the coalition partners) will come back stronger if we go to elections," the Islamist leader said.

Welfare was on the fringe of Turkish politics until this decade, but it won the 1995 electionamid discontent at economic woes. Squabbling among the other parties helped it take the final step to power in months of talks on forming coalitions.

Conservative Ciller has been in government in one way or another since becoming Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993. She had been a strong critic of Welfare but then forged an alliance with it after the Islamists dropped damaging corruption charges against her.

She prevailed upon her Islamist partners to jettison their millenarian "Just Order" of economic and social reform in favour of her free-marketeering ways. The government had targeted a record $4.5 billion in privatisation revenues this year.
But analysts say early polls will kill off plans for a balanced budget in 1997 -- already a remote possibility -- and an assault on annual inflation of around 80 percent.
